utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was there shoulder-to-shoulder [as interpreted] fighting there in the area of Kosare?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the way up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what was the distance between our forces and the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Between 50 and 150 metres, or rather, 50 to 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, how many of your people fell casualty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the entire war within the Pristina Corps, we had 90 soldiers killed and 430 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And in which area did you have the most casualties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Kosare sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- can I clarify one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by shoulder-to-shoulder fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Hand-to-hand combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interpreters corrected it to hand-to-hand, which I do understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, we have combat report from the 125th Brigade from 18th of April, this is the Exhibit Number 5D469 in relation to Kosare and there is a list of died soldiers, and we also have translation of that document in e-court system; so I would like to request admission of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You wish an IC number for the one on the screen first?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you shall have that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say that you have a list of dead soldiers, is that for the Pristina Corps or is that for the 125th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is only for that day from that brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the figure that was given was for the whole of the Pristina Corps, which will be different I think from your list, unless the translation's a problem again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, probably it is a problem in translation because I think the witness clarified that 90 dead and 400 injured are in relation -- were members of their brigade, of 125th Brigade, just from that brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And during the testifying of Witness Filipovic we gave the list and total number of Pristina Corps dead and injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's in the region of 250, is it, or -- is the dead -- the figure for dead somewhere between 2 and 300?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 530 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's my faulty recollection. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And also same meaning of combat report from 125th Brigade which is from 31st of March not in relation to Kosare but in relation to Srbica which number is P2037. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just give me one moment, Mr. Cepic. Yes, I see the evidence of Mr. Filipovic, thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what cooperation did you have with other structures, with civilian authorities, with MUP, with civilian defence, and civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The cooperation was fine to our mutual satisfaction, but under very difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: MUP and civil defence or civilian protection, were any of them resubordinated to you during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not even though I received an order from the commander of the Pristina Corps on the 20th of April or thereabouts that MUP forces in my area of responsibility or in my defence area were resubordinated to me; however, that was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, during the war what signs of recognition did you use?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The usual ones according to the Rules of Service, code and the response code, those were our signs of recognition, of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 699, but unfortunately it is not translated yet, so I would like to mark it for translation and later on I will request their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this not a clear case where it's for you to make a bar table submission later?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. If it's not going to be specifically explored by the witness, then you should apply later for its admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once the war started did you use any bands to denote your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: During the war what was the command of the units like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, command of the units was along the principles of unity of command and singleness of command. The corps commander was my commander, and I was in command of commanders of units. Command unfolded under difficult conditions due to air assaults and other types of assaults, due to disruption of communication lines. So there were situations where I had no contact whatsoever with the corps commander for several days. I also occasionally did not have contact with my battalion commander. There were cases of people bleeding while waiting for assistance because they could not establish contact and ask for assistance to be sent to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, previously during your evidence we saw that members of your unit were familiar with the provisions of the international humanitarian law and the laws of war. Would you please tell me whether that was applied during the war and before the war, of course?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the most important and most frequent issue raised by the corps commander, and naturally all of us. We received a number of documents regulating this, and I on behalf of my unit wrote a number of such orders for prevention purposes. We did not want ourselves to be those who would violate those provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 5D698, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this the document of -- a document of 125th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This military post, 8365, is that your military post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the military post of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We don't need to go through the entire document, but we can see that it deals with the application of regulations in wartime. Would you please tell me, what was the objective of this order and similar orders? What was their purpose?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose was to ensure that anyone who failed to abide by such an order would be subject to disciplinary or criminal measures taken against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We mentioned the bombing. I'd like to know whether in the course of bombing when your forces were bombed, did the NATO aviation use some type of ammunition or some kind of rounds that were not appropriate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I have stated earlier, they used cluster bombs on a number of occasions and they used ammunition with depleted uranium, especially from A-10 aircraft which has a gun of 30-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: There is something that I forgot to ask you, something about Kosare. Just briefly, did you issue a special order to attack Kosare?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, pursuant to a decision by the corps commander. It was my responsibility to issue my own order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Cepic please be asked to speak up. The interpreter can't hear him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you're being asked again by the interpreter to speak more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise one more time. My learned friend Mr. Hannis and me, we discussed about that document, and I think that he hasn't got any objection in relation to the order for Kosare which is the Exhibit Number 5D713, but unfortunately it is not translated yet. May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the one that's on the screen just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which one is it? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has the witness been referred to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, in my previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me a line in the transcript for reference to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Maybe on 51st or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where was it referred to in connection with the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Page 51, lines 6 and 7. I asked him directly in relation: That is the order for Kosare?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the number doesn't appear. Did you actually put the document to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you want it to be marked for identification on the basis there's no objection to it being admitted, you'll need to show it to the witness here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that it now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, simply ask the witness to identify it --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what about this document on the screen in front of you, are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document produced by the command of the 125th Brigade for the action at Kosare.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be marked. That document will be marked --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have him look at the bottom of the document to be sure -- all I see on the screen is the first four paragraphs. I think he should look at the signature and the final page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Cepic, could you deal with that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this your signature or did someone perhaps sign this document on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My mark is there, but it was signed by Zecevic, my assistant commander for the rear. He was authorised to do this on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no problem with that, although it doesn't appear that there's any delivery information. I can address that on cross-exam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. This document will be marked for identification pending translation. Please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what sort of measures did the brigade commander that was in charge take in relation to those who committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, if someone's performance was poor and insufficient, such as was the case of a battalion commander, those people were removed, those men were removed; second, all those who committed crimes were prosecuted under a regular procedure. So much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the name of that commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the commander of the 2nd Light Battalion from the 58th Brigade, my Major Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me if any of the most serious crimes were committed in the 125th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were two or three cases of murder committed by individual members. There were several instances of robbery and about 30 cases of theft. I can't remember the names of any of those involved, but it's all in the survey that was delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This may be a little leading, but let me --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maksimovic, Pesic, and so on and so forth, but not all 30 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in Exhibit P955 there are couple names -- actually all names which General mentioned right now and they are marked also in Exhibit Number P954 as the members of 125th Brigade. Three or four persons for murders and for robberies six or seven and for the thief and for stollen cars roughly 30 persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these documents already exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, one of my last questions: Did you ever receive from General Lazarevic any sort of order, information, or request verbally, in writing requesting that a crime be perpetrated or any of the regulations violated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. These were my questions. Thanks a lot, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. My name is Dan Ivetic and I'm one of the attorneys for Sreten Lukic, and I will be having a couple questions for you this afternoon. First of all, you mentioned and identified the villages of Gornje and Donje Obrinje as being fierce bases for terrorist forces in 1999 in your direct. Was the same true in 1998 with respect to the region and these -- the region surrounding these two villages and these two villages themselves?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall combat operations, joint operations, legitimate joint operations between the MUP and the VJ -- with the MUP and the VJ against the terrorist forces in the greater region surrounding Gornje and Donje Obrinje in the tail end of September 1998, September 26th and onwards?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do. I recall that we were lending support to the MUP forces in that action and we suffered the first losses right there, in terms of combat equipment and manpower. The commander of my combat group, Major Dragan Trifunovic, was wounded in that combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to show you first 6D755 in e-court. This is a document, a combat report of the Pristina Corps dated the 26th of September, 1998, and I would direct your attention to section 2.1 that is visible there at the bottom of the screen both in the English and the Serbian. And it describes that the sabotage and terrorist forces that were surrounded yesterday in the general area of Donje Obrinje and Gornje Obrinje and on the northern slopes of Mount Kosmac put up very fierce resistance during the day (up to now this has been the most fierce resistance offered by the DTS) by firing infantry weapons and head launchers, recoilless guns and 60-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortars from elevated and fortified features in these sectors." Does this report coincide with your recollection based upon your knowledge and experiences of the circumstances, situations, in and around Gornje and Donje Obrinje at the stated time-period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do recall that vividly. This is what the situation was, and the greatest resistance was put up in Gornje and Donje Obrinje in this area including the village of Likovac. Between the village of Likovac and Trdevac, or rather, to the village of Gornje Obrinje to the right and upwards, I witnessed a situation at a distance of about 15 metres when a police vehicle came across an anti-tank mine and was blown up. The mine killed five men and a single person survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I take it then, sir, that the next part of the combat report talking about all approaches into these two villages having been obstructed with mines and explosives and other obstacles, that that also is consistent with your knowledge and experience from the field. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, if we look at the third paragraph in this section which is the last line in the English but in the Serbian it is the -- it's just the third paragraph under section 2 we see a report that: "A large quantity of discarded uniforms, insignia, and weapons of the UCK/KLA were found." Does this coincide with your knowledge and information and recollection about the situation in and around Gornje and Donje Obrinje around September 26, 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the fierce -- with respect to the armed resistance and fighting that the terrorist and sabotage forces in this area were undertaking, am I correct that this lasted for several days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think until the 29th, possibly the 30th of September, so it must have lasted for four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And for our purposes I'd like to show you Exhibit 6D756, another combat report which you'll see once it's up on the screen, sir, of the Pristina Corps command. This one will be dated September 27th, 1998, and I would again direct your attention to section 2 which is there in the middle of the first page on both documents, and ask you if indeed you recall specifically that there was continued resistance and build-up of the forces in the village of Gornje -- of the terrorist forces in the village of Gornje Obrinje itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of resistance and we took over two days to reach Gornje Obrinje from Likovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, in the course of these activities during this time-period, did you have any information about any claimed massacre of many civilians in either Gornje or Donje Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The corps commander at the time, General Pavkovic, requested that I submit a report, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now -- thank you, General. I'd like to move along. With respect to your combat reports, and I think this is moving along to April of 1999, you mentioned -- you mentioned some activities that your forces were involved in in Rugovska Klisura. I'd first like to show you Exhibit P2023, and first of all once the document comes up see if you can recognise this as a document, a regular combat report originating from your brigade and dated the 25th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I mention Rugovska Klisura because there's a section here dealing with Rugovska Klisura right in the middle of the page, and then after that, immediately after that, there is a section dealing with the MUP which is where I would like to ask you and that will be on the next page, page 2 of the English, I apologise, the middle of page 2 of the English which is where section 2 begins, although this is all contained on page 1 of the B/C/S. General, at the time this report was written you reported that five companies of the PJP 73rd Detachment had been incorporated into your brigade and were given posted locations. And then underneath that part you identify the villages where the -- pardon me, the regions where these forces were to be located. And just under that in the Serbian- it's a little difficult to navigate this document in Serbian because there are no paragraph delineations - but just under that section where those villages are identified or those regions I should say, you reported about activities of the terrorist forces in your zone of responsibility and you talk about terrorist combatants in various villages taking off uniforms and posing and civilian refugees in these same villages after combat with the legitimate forces of the state. Was this a tactic of the Albanian terrorist forces that you encountered often?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. When they couldn't cope anymore, they would just change clothes and they would mingle with the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And looking at these villages that are identified here, I think Racaj, Pacaj Seremet, Dobros, et cetera, are you familiar with any of these villages and do they fall within the so-called Caragoj or Reka region surrounding and outside Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with these. It is in the Reka area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now during another part of your direct testimony you talked about how your units had moved out of inhabited settlements pursuant to an order from your superiors. Now, am I correct that although your units moved out there were other units that were not part of either the police or the -- your brigade such -- specifically military territorial detachments of the Ministry of Defence who were mobilised at the beginning of the air war with NATO and situated in various -- in various locations within your zone of defence in 1999. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I recall that there were other units in my zone of defence, as you said, but I'm not sure if they too stayed in settled areas. By mid-April or late April -- I don't remember exactly. I think they all left populated areas by that time. The only units remaining in populated areas were local units such as civil defence and civil protection units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Among these other units, that you say, that were within your zone of defence do you recall the 173rd -- pardon me, the 177th and the 113th Military Territorial Detachments having units in and around Pec and Decani cities controlling the terrain and features in that area? Again, at the beginning of the war, the air war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 113th Military Territorial Detachment was from the Djakovica Military District, or rather, from the Pec Military District but they are from Djakovica and the only unit that I had attached to me was a single company of the 113th. The 177th is from the Pec District. As of mid-April or thereabouts they had abandoned town altogether and took up their defence sectors around the axis roads leading to the town as I had ordered them to because they had been resubordinated to me early [as interpreted] In April.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, I apologise for pausing, sir, I had to wait for the translation and the transcript to catch up with me -- to catch up with us I should say. I apologise, my colleagues have something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you were right the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honour, error in transcript, page 60, line 16, witness said [B/C/S spoken] not early April. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He said what?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: End of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: End of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I just said in Serbian not to clarify with interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He has not then dealt with the question, which was related to the end of March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Can you please repeat the question, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, General. Do you recall at the beginning of the air war, that is to say the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia, that the 177th Military Territorial Detachment with one company of the 113th Military Territorial Detachment was situated in and around Pec and Decani cities conducting control of terrain and specified features in that area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the 113th, I can't say. I can only tell you about the detachment that had been resubordinated to me which was above Decani in the Pobrdje area. Therefore, it was not in a settled area. As for the 177th Detachment, this one had not been resubordinated to me either, and I really don't know where they were at the time. It's late March we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to finish up, do you recall also within your zone that the 180th Military Territorial Detachment was effectuating control in and around the city of Kosovska Mitrovica, including the region from Mitrovica toward Srbica and also toward Zubin Potok and that the 54th Territorial Detachment was situated in and around Vucitrn undertaking the same duties in March -- in the end of March 1999 and onwards?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't help you with that. I don't remember that clearly. I left Kosovska Mitrovica practically altogether. There was a small component that remained behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I will move on and ask you about some of the joint actions to support the MUP forces that you briefly -- that you briefly talked about in direct. I'd like to just clarify a few points, and I'd like to focus for the moment at 1998. Do you recall in 1998, specifically the second half of 1998, that there was a very significant security threat being experienced with the KLA blockading roadways, or as it is in Serbian "komunikacija," in various places within Kosovo and do you recall if your forces were engaged in supporting the MUP to deblockade such roads in August of 1998 in the region of Kramovnik, Boka and Rezina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I recall that. Over 50 per cent of the territory remained under the control of the so-called KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you also recall the participation of your forces along with MUP forces in actions to deblockade the roads in the -- within the region of -- or the line Kramovnik-Boka-Rezina in August 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. At this time if we could call up 6D696. General, I think you will see once this comes up on the screen this to be a decision of the Pristina Corps command dated 30 August 1998 relating to deblockade of roads. And once we get to this -- there we go, that's the cover page -- first page I should say. And if we can turn to page 3 of the Serbian, also page 3 of the English, I think we will see there under section 5.2 the engagement of your unit, the 125th Motorised Brigade, supporting the 8th PJP Detachment and one company of the Djakovica PJP. Does the written assignments and tasks set forth in this decision coincide with your knowledge and recollection of the events as they played out on the ground in the course of this action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I recall this. This is an order by the Pristina Corps commander handing out a set assignment to me, or rather, to the combat group from the 125th, Combat Group 3. It was based on this that I think I eventually drew up an order for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, General, you say that you think it was based on this that you think you eventually drew up an order. Would it have been the regular course and practice within the VJ for yourself upon receiving this -- a decision of this type that you would prepare a decision or a map referencing the assignments of units within your region, both MUP or PJP units and those of the 125th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the practice at the beginning. Very often we did not receive excerpts based on maps attached to documents such as these. We had to do them ourselves in order to know for sure -- for the commander of combat group 3 to know exactly where it was headed, where he should go, where he was to link up and meet up with the commander of the 8th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, I apologise for the delay. We're waiting for the transcript. If we could take a moment briefly to look at 6D676 then, I think you can be in a position to identify whether this map, in fact, is one that you prepared for this particular action. Is that, in fact, the case, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this map was drafted in the Pec garrison on the base of the order of the Pristina Corps command, and it was sent to the commander of the 3rd combat group.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to this particular action, am I correct that then both yourself and the police superior officers conducted this action in accordance with the assignments specified on this map order? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there personally. The commander of the 3rd combat group was there and he coordinated the action or supported, actually, the 8th Detachment and coordinated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was it assigned these identification numbers to the various MUP companies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It's a MUP formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that had the tasks and assignments specified in the order and in the map not been carried out successfully, that would be reflected in a written combat report generated by the army commander who was the one leading the army forces in that action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the army commander commanded or led the action? No, actually. The army commander supported the action; and had he not done that, the report would have reached me and I would have had to inform the commander, General Pavkovic, that the action was not carried out because I received the order from General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... verified for us that if any action were not -- strike that. Would that be true for any action if any action were not successfully completed or had had any problems affecting its completion there would be a written report generated and sent back up the chain in the VJ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that for me I need to report back that my commander's order I was not able to execute, and then I would note the reasons for this. I don't know if we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would briefly like to move to 1999 just to touch on a few points of a similar nature. First of all, I have a document, albeit drafted by a different brigade, but involving assignments for a portion of your forces. If we can call up 5D794. This is an order originating from the 7th Infantry Brigade dated May 5th, 1999, for an action in smashing the STS in the region of Trbuhovac, Doljac, Ruhot, Pobrdje, and Trstenik. And if you look at section 2 of the document on the first page in B/C/S and I believe on the second page of -- I take that back, it should be on the first page of the English as well I think according to my notes. Yeah, it starts on the first page and goes to the second page in English. You'll see assignments for the 125th Brigade along with the PJP to undertake to smash or attack forces in a certain direction. Do you recall this action; and if so did the planned assignments set forth here in this "zapovest" actually get carried out on the terrain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I must admit that I don't recall this at all because this is an order from my colleague, the 7th Brigade commander, I didn't receive it, and it is mentioned here that a part of the 125th unit forces. I don't know perhaps if the platoon from the Pec military department was engaged in the attack on a part of that road, otherwise I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think to the last exhibit that I'd like to ask you about, P2157. This is a "naredjenje," order, originating from the 125th Motorised Brigade dated the 6th of June, 1999, regarding control of roads and territory in the zone of responsibility of your brigade. Looking first at the top right it would appear that a copy was sent to the command of the 23rd PJP. Do you recall such an order giving assignments to both military and MUP units? And to be fair, if you need to turn to the second and final page of this document, by all means just say so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my order, but this is an agreement with the security chief who went together with the MUP because we didn't want me to be ordering something which could be perhaps improper because they were not subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And this order was actually effectuated on the terrain by both the military and MUP units, as written in this order; is that accurate then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the roads in our sectors, and we're controlling them via these detachments. And where we were not able to do that we would ask for help from the MUP and that's when they were attached and were executing or effectuating their assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thanks, General. Let me just check one thing and I will see if I have one or two further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have no further questions for you, and I'm reminded that I went over the time for a break perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- so I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no problem with that, Mr. Ivetic, to completely the cross-examination. We have to have another break now, Mr. Zivanovic, so could you again leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good evening, General. Can you tell us a little bit about your VJ background --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you first join the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you still active duty or have you retired?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I retired on the 31st of March, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At what rank?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Major-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I know this is not your first time in The Hague. I understand you testified in the Haradinaj case last fall, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to start by asking you about the Joint Command, and I'd like to show you an Exhibit Number P2113. I believe you'll recognise this one. It's dated the 7th of July, 1998, and hopefully it will be on your screen in a minute. We can go to the second page which has your signature just for a second in a B/C/S, if we may. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the English translation has this document headed as: "Ban on operations without the knowledge and approval of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." And it says: "Pursuant to the Order of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, Strictly Confidential Number 1104-6 of 6 July 1998 ..." And so on. Let me ask you something about the numbering system. That -- we've had evidence about how VJ documents are numbered and recorded in registers or log-books. This number, 1104-6, in 1998 did you know to what unit or what part of the VJ that register number pertained?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, you said in the heading "ban on operations," actually it's not operations but on actions. Second, this number, I assume that it's the number from the Pristina Corps command because I refer back to that document. I cannot make up my own numbers. I don't really have any numbers of superior commands unless it's something that is contained in a document that I receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I will tell you I think we'll probably see later on, we do have some Pristina Corps documents from 1998 which have that four-digit number, 1104. But if your order here you say: "Pursuant to the Order of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija ..." Why did you not write: Pursuant to the order of the Pristina Corps, if you thought that's where it was coming from? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a subordinate to the Pristina Corps command do not have the right to change the heading of a document received from a superior command. So in the preamble I have to refer back to that number if I mean to adhere to the procedure. Sometimes if this is not -- sometimes we omit drafting the introductory part of the document so then we don't refer to anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That answer's not very clear to me, Mr. Hannis. Whether it's based on the number or the actual statement that you put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm going to follow-up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I understand what you're saying then, General, it sounds like confidential number 1104-6, which we do not have here, we haven't seen that document, it sounds like when you got it, it had at the top: "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija," correct? That's why you wrote this this way, because the document you received said "Joint Command" not "Pristina Corps." Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Most probably that's what it is. I mean, I cannot make up my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I agree. If that order had said "Pristina Corps command" at the top, you would have said: Pursuant to order of the Pristina Corps command number 1104-6, right, you wouldn't have changed it to "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would not change it. I am not allowed to change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when you first heard the term "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the term, and I asked what this was about and this is why I wanted to hear personally from the commander, and he wasn't there, so I called the operations officer and he explained to me, It's all right. It's a document from the Pristina Corps command, act pursuant to it, and in future you can act pursuant to all the documents containing this term in the same way that you would do with documents coming from the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So then I take it this was the first time you saw or heard that term "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" was when you received that order dated the 6th of July, 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is why I called the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you called him because you'd never seen that term before and that was something unusual, Joint Command; and "command" is a term that has significance for military personnel, right, and you wanted to know what that was all about. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it like that, because it was illogical. I received an explanation that this was coordinated at the highest level and that this is support by the VJ to the MUP forces, and that in future I would be receiving things like this without signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you make that phone call before you issued this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it then you called either the same day or the very next day after you got the order. Who did you talk to since the commander wasn't available? Do you know who the person was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The moment the Joint Command document came to me I tried to get the commander and I couldn't, I got the operations officer, at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who that person was by name or by rank?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely I know the operative officer was Colonel Milan Djakovic at the time; now he's a retired general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- so then you issued this order to your subordinate units, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I think that it says there to the combat groups, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I see here on the right it says something that's translated as: "BG-4," I take it that's Combat Group 4. Does that mean -- did you send it to all your subordinate units or only to BG-4, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would need to look at the end of the document to see if there's a list of all the recipients.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can tell you there's nothing on this copy as far as delivery information. Did any of your subordinate units call you and say, What's this Joint Command? Did any of them ask you about Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at this point. They asked that later because they were not able to ask, because in the heading it says the command of the 125th Motorised Brigade so they know or they knew who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, before coming here to testify in this case between the end of the war -- well, between this conversation with Colonel Djakovic and coming here to testify, did you ever discuss with anybody else the Joint Command, about what it was or who was a member of it? Did you ever have any conversation like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any specific requests to have this explained to me. When I saw Djakovic again and on subsequent occasions also the commander, it was explained to me that this was the -- a support to the MUP forces. And when we provided this support, the commander of the combat group and the detachment commander would find themselves in one place; and from that place everyone would command their own units and according to some instructions or regulations we would call that a combined command post and the action performed from that combined command post location is called a joint exercise of command. I don't know if I'm being clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that's precisely the answer I was looking for. After -- did you follow any of the proceedings in the Slobodan Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I did see some footage once, but I was not really prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 73, 1, I believe the witness said joint commanding, not Joint Command, I mean just for the clarity of the transcript because it says this action would be called joint commanding, that is what he said, at least in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will ask the CLSS to review the tape and give us a clarification of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And have you followed any of the proceedings in this case on TV or in the newspaper or through interested persons in Serbia before coming here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in newspapers and in reports, I spoke with several colleagues about how our colleagues were holding up here, our superiors, and also while preparing for this testimony now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a result of that, did you become aware that this issue about the Joint Command was a controversial issue in this case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that it is a controversial issue, but it's clear to me, it's clear to me what this document is. It's a document from the corps command, and it was always clear that that's what it was, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Cepic earlier mentioned that you had held an instruction or teaching post. Can you clarify that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did teach for two years the topic of -- or the subject of strategy as part of the military teaching institutions, and this is why earlier I mentioned these two terms, combined commanding and joint commanding. So a combined command post would be the place, the location; while joint commanding is an action, it's a verb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is this a recognised military term, joint commanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not in the instructions on the work of the staff commands, but there is the term combined command post, so we added as soon as the command post was combined that is the place where joint commanding is carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But of course the words that we are considering here are not joint commanding but Joint Command, that's what the documents record. Can you envisage yourself as a military instructor explaining to students or soldiers who are being given instruction what "Joint Command" means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can imagine it, but it's hard to explain, I mean it's hard to explain it here as well because it's something that is not, like I said, in the military literature. But it's a word that was put together and that is clear to me in terms of the explanation that I provided earlier. It's the command of the Pristina Corps, and this is something that we acted pursuant to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us another example of the use of the words "Joint Command" from your Yugoslav military experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot give you anything about Joint Command, but I can give you something about the coordinating body, coordinating staff, joint staff. As for Joint Command, it's something that I have not encountered in my earlier practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In view of what we've been told about the importance of singleness of command or unity of command in the Yugoslav Army structure, is the expression "Joint Command" not actually illogical and inherently contradictory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, formally from a legal standpoint it could be a bit unusual. But as a consequence it did not pose a problem in the hierarchy of singleness, of unity, of command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interpreter would like you to repeat the last part of that answer, Mr. Zivanovic. You said that it could be seen as a bit unusual, but could you tell us what you said after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, it was not a problem for me in the second part because I obeyed my commander. As far as I was concerned, it was a document from my commander and I would obey my superior commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's easy for me, and I suspect, for others to understand the concept of a combined command post and to understand the idea of senior officers of the MUP and the VJ being in the same place and making sure that the orders they gave to their respective forces were not inconsistent. That's simple, I think. But "Joint Command" I have much greater difficulty with because it seems to be important to the army officers who have given here -- who have given evidence here to distinguish that in some way as not involving jointness of command. It's explained always here as the opposite, that the command is never joined, the command is always kept separate; and therefore, it is very difficult for an outsider trying to understand this to see why, when it was important to keep these commands separate, they're called "Joint Command." Can you help me any further in trying to unravel this dilemma?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's difficult for me, too, to understand, never mind explain it to you; but I will try to do that if you permit me. There are two structures which are treated in these documents of the Joint Command, this is the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP. To this day, if you put them into a parallel position, perhaps in this room, to agree on an action it would be very difficult for them to do that. There must be somebody above them who would coordinate that. I didn't go into that. I assumed when I put my question -- Djakovic said this was something that was done at the highest level about coordination between the MUP and the army. So the way I understood it was that there was somebody who was higher up who was coordinating it and saying, All right, MUP, you will do this; and army, you will do this, along the line of the Chief of Staff [as interpreted]. This is how I understood it. I don't know if I have been clear enough. It's an unfortunate formulation, so it's a bit difficult also for me to understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're helping me. I'm getting closer, I think. Mr. Hannis, would you like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: One little thing more I wanted to request you for clarification. Now, if they were sitting in the same place jointly acting on some action, whose order were these two different entities, if they were not merged together, if they were different entities, whose orders were they implementing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that at the top it was the minister of the interior and Chief of the General Staff who made an agreement between themselves. I wouldn't be able to tell you anything further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we need to correct something that the General said. Page 77, line 4, it says here "Chief of Staff," whereas the General said "Chief of General Staff," not just any staff. That's what he meant when he said it was at a high level, otherwise it might appear that it was a chief of some lower unit such as brigade or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that explanation of the translation, Mr. Fila. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, yes, I think that is helpful. You've suggested that somebody higher up who was coordinating it. And among the possibilities, who was higher up that would have that kind of power or authority or control over both the army and the MUP in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There always is somebody higher up, somebody at the top. I think that it was either in late June or early July that a session of the Supreme Defence Council was held where a decision was made that the Army of Yugoslavia was to participate in support of MUP forces aimed at combatting terrorist forces. That was a decision made at the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a practical matter in real life, in 1998 and 1999, isn't it true that Slobodan Milosevic was the one man in Yugoslavia who would have that kind of power over both the army and Ministry of Interior? Is there anybody else that was higher than him with regard to those two?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. Very well. The Supreme Defence Council that was the highest body comprising three persons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, with all due respect towards Mr. Hannis, hasn't it been made clear that 1998 and the state of war in 1999 are not the same things. And when Mr. Hannis puts a question like he did just now, that confuses people. Supreme Defence Council was in 1999 -- 1998, whereas 1999 is something quite different. So I think that the Prosecutor needs to first put his questions about 1998 and then about the state of war because it's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not going to rule against you on this, Mr. Hannis, for a number of reasons based on the lack of clarity in evidence about the change, if any, that occurred in March 1999 and the status of the Supreme Defence Council. However, it's a matter for you to consider whether you really will get the best out of this issue by asking such a broad question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. Well, for Mr. Fila I can break it down into two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 before the state of war was declared, isn't it true Mr. Milosevic was the one person in Yugoslavia who had that kind of power, to control both the army, the VJ, and the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia? And I'm talking real life. I'm not talking something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of course you are, Mr. -- and I certainly understand that. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, I have a principled objection to this kind of question. General Zivanovic is a fact witness here not an expert witness who is an expert in politics. I think the General can only give us relevant information about his brigade and the activities that he conducted within the Pristina Corps and not about something that transpired at a much higher level. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That objection is repelled. Mr. Hannis, a senior army officer is clearly in a position to be presented with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do I need to repeat my question or do you recall it and can you answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite it because you phrased it in the following terms: Isn't it. Could you put it in a different form, please, because then it would be clear for me. Don't phrase it as a negative, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, all right. Who was the most powerful in Yugoslavia in terms of control over the army in 1998 and 1999 before the state of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The most powerful man in terms of control of the army was the Chief of the General Staff, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who did the Chief of General Staff answer to? Who could replace him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was the president of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; at that time it was Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you aware of any vote in the Supreme Defence Council where the Supreme Defence Council decided contrary to anything that Mr. Milosevic wanted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't familiar with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. I was just informed about what happened in June; but no, I'm not familiar with it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, what's your understanding of the position of the Supreme Defence Council in relation to control of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not quite sure. I think that they have no competences in peacetime just in wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So now you'll see the point of Mr. Hannis addressing you on this issue the way he has, so please try to assist us as best you can. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're aware, General, that the Chief of Staff of the army in the first part of 1998 was General Perisic, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he was removed and replaced -- well, he was replaced because he went to another job, he was replaced by the Supreme Defence Council. You know that, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if you're aware that in the Supreme Defence Council session in which that was discussed that President -- the president of Montenegro was opposed to the change but Mr. Milosevic wanted to have a different general as Chief of the General Staff, and that was General Ojdanic. So are you aware of that, that there was some dispute within the Supreme Defence Council, but Mr. Milosevic got his way?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to intervene at this point. We heard the evidence over here on multiple occasions of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. Just a moment. Mr. Zivanovic, while we deal with this matter, would you please leave the courtroom. It's not appropriate you should hear any legal argument on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, 81, 16, my learned friend Mr. Hannis is, I believe, putting a witness in an awkward position because he's misinterpreting the actual facts. Mr. Perisic was not replaced by the decision of the Supreme Defence Council but by the decision of the president of FRY, which according to the constitution is the only person who can replace, remove, appoint, and everything else what he can do with the army officers. So in that case, in that case, also the suggestion that there was a dispute at the Supreme Defence Council, we have seen that, but this is irrelevant. So I believe that my friend, Mr. Hannis, is by his question is misleading the witness and that is the basis of my objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, actually, Your Honour, I think that makes my argument stronger --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say that's how it seems to me, but nevertheless the question of accuracy arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess the constitution as I understand it says the president has the power to do that in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I don't think it does in relation to promotion or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay you're right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Or removal of generals --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's correct. That's correct. That's entirely his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So while it may clarify the point you're trying to make in one sense, it does mean that the arguments that are advanced by opponents of that view are simply I suppose advisory and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll leave that. I don't think I need to pursue that any further with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's have the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, thank you for your patience. The matter has been dealt with. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, are you aware of who the minister of the interior was in 1998 for the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know who Jovica Stanisic was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know from the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did he stop being the minister of interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean Vlajko?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. When did Mr. Stojiljkovic become minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say that. I truly don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know when Jovica Stanisic was replaced in his position within the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Was it in 1999? I don't know. I don't focus on these political figures. I know the ministers but not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to some other military documents. I want to show you P1427. This is a Pristina Corps command forward command post document entitled: "Decision on the joint engagement of MUP and VJ forces." It's dated the 10th of August, 1998. And if we could go to the last page of the B/C/S you'll see it's signed by General Pavkovic. And among the addressees is the 125th Motorised Brigade. Do you recall having received this document in August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you will see above General Pavkovic's signature in item number 6 about command and communications it says: "Combat operations will be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from the Pristina Corps forward command post in Djakovica." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And isn't it true that in August of 1998 General -- Colonel -- then the head of the forward command post was General Lazarevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Lazarevic was colonel at the time. Perhaps he was general in August and he was the commander of the forward command post in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but he was the -- he was the Chief of Staff and he was the ranking officer at the forward command post for the Pristina Corps at that time, was he not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, within the group which was at the forward command post in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think on page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S you'll see in item 2.4 that there was a task for the 125th to support or in a coordinated action engage with the 10th MUP Detachment in attacking along a certain axis, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is just one combat group of the 125th Motorised Brigade that was supposed to act in coordinated action with MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, next I want to show you a document from four days later. This is P1428, if we could have it up in e-court, please. This is from the Pristina Corps command and it's dated the 14th of August entitled: "A decision on breaking up DTS, sabotage and terrorist forces, in the Slup and Voksa villages sector." General, do you recall having received this document in August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see in item 2.2 that there is a task for Battle Group 2 of the 125th to carry out a diversionary attack, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here, to carry out a diversionary attack to the south-east of Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 of the English and the last page, page 4, of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll see under item 6 the indication that: "Combat operations will be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija," it's translated here as, "with the Pristina Corps, forward command post, in Djakovica." Could you read that out for me. I want to make sure that translation is correct.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "Command of combat actions shall be carried out by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the fourth page of the English and on the page in B/C/S in front of you, we see it has the typed name and a signature of Colonel Lazarevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So on the 14th of August, Colonel -- then-Colonel Lazarevic is signing an order which directs that combat operations will be commanded by the Joint Command. Did you -- did your subordinate unit carry out that action, do you recall, in the Slup and Voksa action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This Combat Group 2 was there, and practically it didn't engage in any important activities. Most likely, the corps commander authorised General Lazarevic to sign the order. This is a document of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, actually, we have evidence that he did more than that. We have General Pavkovic speaking at a meeting of the Joint Command, indicating that this action in Slup and Voksa will be commanded by Colonel Lazarevic. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you have not ever seen the minutes or the notes of meetings of the Joint Command, some 65-plus meetings between July 22nd and October of 1998? No one's ever shown that document to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I saw this document once -- rather, I saw several sentences here during the Haradinaj trial, I saw it in e-court. Now, whether that came from that command or elsewhere, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Colonel Djakovic ever tell you that he took notes of those Joint Command meetings in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. There was no reason or need for him to tell me that. I was subordinated to the corps command and it was my duty to obey them, to do what they tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If in these actions there was a necessity for you or your subordinate units to coordinate with the MUP, how was that done? Physically how did you accomplish that? Did you call the MUP commander in or did he come see you? Typically how was that done, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Once we receive a document to support the MUP forces, then we agreed on whether I would meet with the chief of the secretariat of the interior, say from Pec, depending whether it was carried out, or the commander of the combat group and the detachment that he was supposed to support, we're going to meet and then they would arrange it among themselves in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion in 1998 or 1999 to travel to Pristina to meet with MUP officers to coordinate actions like this, anti-terrorist actions in which the VJ was going to support and work together with the MUP in carrying them out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did stay there several times in July and August, I don't remember any longer, but that was at the invitation and order of the corps commander, General Pavkovic. And according to the official rules, I would go and see him in his office or wherever he said he would be. I have to tell you that it wasn't easy for me to go to report to the commander because I would always expect on those occasions that I would be given a specific assignment that would be quite difficult. If I may add, and he's here present listening to this, I would always say that I would fare badly following such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were all those meetings then in - did you say in July and August - were all those one-on-one meetings with General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the custom used by General Pavkovic, he would always call commanders individually and they would meet tete-a-tete. And only when we had joint briefings would we all meet together with the commander. Commander General Pavkovic was frequently on the move and he came to Kosovska Mitrovica much more often than I came to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We had evidence from another brigade commander about in 1998 in connection with these kind of anti-terrorist actions in support of the MUP that there were meetings in Pristina which both VJ commanders and MUP commanders met, at which General Pavkovic and I think he said General Lukic from the MUP were present. Did you ever attend a meeting like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never attended such a meeting. Pursuant to an order from Pavkovic, after staying in his offices or in the building of the command, once or twice I was sent to see certain people I guess in the MUP. Once it was to meet the chief of police from Belgrade who was in Pec at the time, his name was Ignjatovic, and it concerned actions in Dus and Sicevo. The second time it was to meet with, I guess, Colonel -- perhaps Andric, who was there in the Djakovica-Decani sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. General, did you ever hear in 1998 a group or an organ or a body called the Operations Inter-Departmental Staff For the Suppression of Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija? Did you ever hear of that group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not then. I heard that here while being proofed here and I read minutes from one of the meetings, but I had never heard of it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of such a group by any other name that included VJ, MUP, and political -- high-ranking political personnel dealing with the problem of suppressing terrorism in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear of it. I suppose that it had to be discussed in certain circles, and then the public had to be informed, but I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the so-called plan for combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija or sometimes we've heard it referred to as the five-phase plan for combatting terrorism. Did you ever hear of those terms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No -- rather, yes, I heard that from the corps commander. He mentioned that when meeting me or other commanders somewhere on the ground and he would say, Now we're in the phase of anti-terrorist combat, but I don't know whether it was the second phase or the third one. I never received a document specifying what phase it was. But to tell you the truth, I was never interested in it because I had much more important problems to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you would agree with me, though, if it was important to your commander, General Pavkovic, to a certain degree it was important to you as well, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to me it didn't matter what stage this was. The only important thing for me was what my assignment was and what I had to carry out. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall attending a meeting in June, early June 1998, to discuss combat-readiness in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible, but I can't remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me move to another document then.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We met several times in Prizren and then in Djakovica to deal with problems related to securing the state border. I'm not sure which one you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we look at Exhibit P2098 just before we have a break, General. This is a document dated the 5th of June, 1998, from the Pristina Corps command and it's an order regarding measures to increase the level of combat-readiness. And the first paragraph says: "On 5 June 1998 at Djakovica forward command post... The implementation of combat and other tasks was analysed. All the commanders of the units first in subordination (BG)," which I understand is combat groups, "in the area of Djakovica were present." Do you recall attending that meeting seeing this now.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall whether these were commanders of combat groups or subordinate units. I was not the brigade commander at the time. I was the brigade Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be an appropriate place for me to stop for now, if that's agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Zivanovic, we have to interrupt for the day at this stage; that means that you need to return tomorrow to complete your evidence. The court will be sitting tomorrow at 9.00, and that will be in Courtroom I. So you should be back in time to re-commence at that stage. Meanwhile it's very important that between now and then you have absolutely no communication whatsoever with any person about the evidence in this case, either the evidence that's been heard so far or the evidence that might yet be given. You must confine any communications or discussions to matters that do not relate to this case. Please bear that in mind and now please also leave the courtroom with the usher, and we'll see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 18th day of January, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
